title: Museum Island in Berlin: which museum to choose for two hours, and which ticket to buy
subtitle: Five museums on one island, one of them closed for years. How to pick one, and what each kind of ticket opens.
excerpt: Museum Island in Berlin has five museums and most visitors have time for one. What each house holds, what the closure of the Pergamon Museum means, and how the single, island and combined tickets differ.
longtail_phrases: which museum on Museum Island is best
is the Pergamon Museum in Berlin closed
where is the bust of Nefertiti in Berlin
how long do you need on Museum Island
is there one ticket for all museums on Museum Island
meta_title: Museum Island Berlin: which museum, which ticket
meta_description: Five museums, one closed for years. Which house on Museum Island to choose for two hours, where Nefertiti is, and what each kind of ticket opens.

featured_image.alt: The domed Bode Museum at the tip of Museum Island in Berlin at dusk, with the river Spree and the television tower

content_html:
[place attraction="museum-island" city="berlin"]

On 6 December 1912, in the ruins of a sculptor's workshop at Amarna in Egypt, a German excavation lifted a painted limestone head out of the rubble: a queen in a tall blue crown, with one eye left blank. The dig was paid for by James Simon, a Berlin cotton merchant. The bust of Nefertiti stood in his house for some years before he gave it to the city's museums in 1920.

The building where she was first shown to the public, the Neues Museum, was bombed in the Second World War and stood as a ruin for more than sixty years. The bust spent the last weeks of the war in a salt mine and the following decades in West Berlin. Building and bust were reunited in October 2009. The island she came back to has five museums and one entrance building, and most visitors have time for one house, or two at most. So the choice matters.

The island in brief

Museum Island is the northern tip of an island in the river Spree, in the middle of Berlin. Its five museums were built one after another between 1830 and 1930 for the collections of the Prussian kings, and the whole group has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1999.

The lawns, the colonnades and the riverside paths are free to walk. Each museum has its own door and its own ticket check. The white building with thin columns beside the canal is the James-Simon-Galerie, opened in 2019 and named after the man who paid for the dig: it holds ticket desks, a cloakroom and a café.

The James-Simon-Galerie, the entrance building of the island, opened in 2019. Photo: Leonhard Lenz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

First, the bad news: the Pergamon Museum is closed

The largest and best-known museum of the island has been completely closed since October 2023 for a rebuilding that is planned in stages over many years. The Pergamon Altar, the Ishtar Gate of Babylon and the Market Gate of Miletus cannot be seen. Do not plan a visit around them without checking first.

Across the canal from the island, a separate exhibition building called Pergamonmuseum. Das Panorama has been showing a painted 360 degree view of the ancient city by the artist Yadegar Asisi, together with some original sculptures. It is worth knowing about, and it is not the museum.

Which museum for your two hours

Neues Museum: Egypt and Nefertiti

The first choice for most people. It holds the Egyptian collection, with the bust of Nefertiti alone in a domed room at the north end, and the collections of prehistory, among them a tall cone of beaten gold from the Bronze Age known as the Berlin Gold Hat. The building is part of the visit: the architect David Chipperfield repaired the ruin without hiding its damage, so burnt brick and bullet marks sit beside new plain walls. Photographing the bust is not allowed.

The staircase hall of the Neues Museum, rebuilt plain inside the old brick walls. Photo: Yair Haklai, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Alte Nationalgalerie: paintings

The temple on a high base holds nineteenth-century painting: Caspar David Friedrich's Monk by the Sea, Adolph Menzel's scenes of Prussian life and work, and a room of French Impressionists. If you would choose pictures over statues, come here. Ninety minutes are enough.

The colonnade that runs round the garden of the Alte Nationalgalerie. Photo: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE.

Altes Museum: Greeks and Romans

Karl Friedrich Schinkel's building of 1830, with eighteen columns facing the Lustgarten, was the first museum on the island. Inside are Greek, Etruscan and Roman antiquities around a rotunda modelled on the Pantheon in Rome. It is the smallest visit: an hour to an hour and a half.

The Altes Museum across the Lustgarten. The lawn is free, and full on any warm day. Photo: Bahnfrend, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Bode Museum: sculpture and quiet

The domed building at the tip of the island holds European sculpture from the Middle Ages onward, Byzantine art and one of the great coin collections. It is the least visited of the five, which on a crowded day is a reason to choose it.

How the tickets work

  • A ticket for one museum is entry to that house on one day. For the Neues Museum it is usually tied to a time slot.
  • An island ticket covers all the museums of the island that are open, on a single day. It pays for itself with the second museum, if you have the legs for it.
  • A museum pass for Berlin runs for several days and covers many museums across the city. It makes sense on a longer stay.
  • Visitors under eighteen go into the state museums free, but still need a ticket for a time slot where slots are used.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Museum Island ticket with a city audio tour lists entry to the island's museums and an audio walk through the centre of Berlin. Its own notes say the commentary does not cover the inside of the museums.
  • The Neues Museum ticket with an audio tour and a city walk is the one listing here whose commentary goes through the museum's halls.
  • Listings that pair a walk through Berlin with a ticket to the Altes Museum, the Bode Museum or the Neues Museum include entry and an audio walk outside. Inside you are on your own.
  • The walk with a ticket to the Panorama names a ticket in its title, while its list of inclusions mentions only the audio tour. Read what is written before you pay.
  • Plain entrance tickets to single museums are sold too, without any audio.

These are the Museum Island tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="berlin" match="island,island,neues,altes,bode,pergamon" limit="8"]

Practical notes

  • Most of the museums are closed on Mondays, and some on a second day. The current days and hours are on our page for Museum Island.
  • The underground station Museumsinsel, on line U5, is at the southern edge of the island. The S-Bahn station Hackescher Markt is five minutes away on foot.
  • Coats and bags go into the cloakroom or lockers. Large rucksacks are not allowed in the rooms.
  • Go at opening time, or in the last two hours of the day. The Nefertiti room is at its fullest around midday.

From here

The Berlin Cathedral stands on the same island, beside the Lustgarten. It is not one of the state museums and has its own ticket, which includes the climb to the dome. Unter den Linden starts at the bridge and leads west to the Brandenburg Gate in about twenty minutes on foot. For the rest of Berlin, or to fit it into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Which museum on Museum Island should you choose?
faqs.a: With two hours, the Neues Museum, for the Egyptian collection and the bust of Nefertiti. Choose the Alte Nationalgalerie if you prefer paintings, the Altes Museum for Greek and Roman art, and the Bode Museum for sculpture and fewer people.

faqs.q: Is the Pergamon Museum in Berlin open?
faqs.a: No. It has been completely closed since October 2023 for a rebuilding planned in stages over many years, so the Pergamon Altar and the Ishtar Gate cannot be seen. A separate Panorama exhibition across the canal is not the museum.

faqs.q: Where is the bust of Nefertiti in Berlin?
faqs.a: In the Neues Museum on Museum Island, alone in a domed room at the north end of the Egyptian collection. Photographing it is not allowed.

faqs.q: Is there one ticket for all the museums on Museum Island?
faqs.a: Yes. An island ticket covers all the museums of the island that are open, on one day. Single tickets for one museum are sold as well.

faqs.q: How long do you need on Museum Island?
faqs.a: About two hours for the Neues Museum and an hour to an hour and a half for each of the others. Two museums are a full half day.

title: Seeing Klimt's Kiss in Vienna: which Belvedere to book, and which art museum to choose after it
subtitle: The painting is in one of three Belvedere buildings. Then the choice is between Bruegel and the state rooms of a palace.
excerpt: Where exactly Klimt's Kiss hangs in Vienna and which Belvedere ticket you need for it, how the Kunsthistorisches Museum and the Albertina compare if you have time for one more, and what the partner's tickets include.
focus_keyword: where to see Klimt's Kiss in Vienna
longtail_phrases: where is Klimt's Kiss in Vienna
is The Kiss in the Upper or Lower Belvedere
which art museum in Vienna is best
Kunsthistorisches Museum or Albertina
are the Belvedere gardens free
meta_title: Klimt's Kiss in Vienna: which Belvedere, which museum
meta_description: The Kiss hangs in the Upper Belvedere, one of three Belvedere buildings. Which ticket you need, and how Vienna's other great art museums compare.

featured_image.alt: The Upper Belvedere palace in Vienna reflected in its pond at dusk

content_html:
[place attraction="belvedere-vienna" city="vienna"]

In the summer of 1908 Gustav Klimt and his friends put up a temporary exhibition hall in Vienna and filled it with their own work. One room was Klimt's. On its wall hung a square canvas, not quite finished, of a couple kneeling at the edge of a meadow, wrapped in gold. He called it The Lovers.

A few years earlier the same city had quarrelled bitterly over the ceiling paintings he made for its university, and he had sworn never again to work for the state. Yet the state bought the new picture straight from the exhibition, for its modern gallery, before the paint was done. The Kiss has belonged to that gallery ever since, and the gallery does not lend it. To see it you have to come to Vienna, and to the right one of three buildings.

Which Belvedere: Upper, Lower or 21

The Belvedere is two baroque palaces at either end of a sloping garden, built by Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt for Prince Eugene of Savoy, the general who commanded the Habsburg armies. The Lower Belvedere, where he lived, came first. The Upper Belvedere, finished in 1723, was for show. A third building, Belvedere 21, is a modern pavilion some way off.

  • The Upper Belvedere holds the permanent collection, and The Kiss. This is the ticket you need.
  • The Lower Belvedere shows temporary exhibitions, in and beside the prince's own state rooms.
  • Belvedere 21 shows contemporary art.
  • The garden between the two palaces is free.

Tickets for the Upper Belvedere are sold for a time slot, and the popular hours fill up in season. A ticket for one building does not open the others unless it says so.

Inside the Upper Belvedere

The Kiss hangs on the upper floor, among the largest group of Klimt's paintings anywhere, including his Judith of 1901. It is 180 centimetres square, painted in oil with gold leaf laid on, and it has a wall to itself. The crowd in front of it changes every few minutes, so wait at the side for a clear view.

The Kiss, finished in 1908. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere and is not lent. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Do not leave straight after. The same floor has Egon Schiele's The Embrace and Death and the Maiden, and elsewhere in the building are the grimacing heads carved by Franz Xaver Messerschmidt in the eighteenth century. In the Marble Hall at the centre, on 15 May 1955, the foreign ministers of the four occupying powers signed the treaty that gave Austria back its independence. Allow an hour and a half.

One picture you will not find: the gold portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, which hung here for decades. It was returned to the family's heirs in 2006 and is now in New York.

If you have time for one more museum

The Kunsthistorisches Museum: old masters

The domed palace on the Ring, opened in 1891, was built to show what the Habsburgs had collected over four centuries. Its picture gallery has the largest group of paintings by Pieter Bruegel the Elder in the world, twelve panels, with the Tower of Babel, the Peasant Wedding and the Hunters in the Snow in one room. Close by are Vermeer's Art of Painting, Raphael's Madonna of the Meadow and the portraits Velázquez painted of the Spanish infantas.

Klimt is here too. On the great staircase, look up between the arches and columns: the figures were painted by him, his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch in 1890 and 1891, long before the gold. This is the largest of the three museums: two hours for the paintings alone.

Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow, of 1565, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum. Photo: reproduction of a painting in the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Kunsthistorisches Museum across Maria-Theresien-Platz, with the monument to the empress. Photo: Manfred Werner (Tsui), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The Albertina: a palace and its drawings

The Albertina stands on a bastion behind the State Opera. It was the palace of Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen, who founded the collection in 1776, and its fame rests on prints and drawings, above all Dürer's Young Hare of 1502. Works on paper fade in light, so the hare is shown only rarely, and what you see most of the time is a copy.

What is always on view: some twenty Habsburg state rooms, and a permanent hanging of modern painting from Monet to Picasso. Its second house, the Albertina Modern on Karlsplatz, shows art made after 1945.

The Hall of the Muses, one of the state rooms of the Albertina. Photo: Thomas Ledl, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In short

  • For Klimt and Vienna around 1900: the Upper Belvedere.
  • For Bruegel, Vermeer and the old masters: the Kunsthistorisches Museum.
  • For palace rooms and Monet to Picasso in an hour: the Albertina.

What the partner's listings include

  • The Upper Belvedere ticket with a highlights audio tour and a city walk includes entry, commentary on the main works of the permanent collection in the partner's app, and an audio walk outside. Special exhibitions are not covered.
  • The Kunsthistorisches Museum ticket with a highlights audio tour includes entry and about an hour of commentary on the main works.
  • The Albertina Palace ticket with an audio tour includes entry, but the commentary covers the state rooms only. Its own notes exclude the art collection.
  • The Albertina Palace audio tour is the same commentary without a ticket. You buy entry yourself.
  • The Albertina Modern ticket with a city walk includes entry and an audio walk outside, with no commentary inside.
  • An entry ticket for all Albertina locations is listed without details. Check which houses it names.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for these museums, with today's prices:

[partner city="vienna" match="belvedere,kunsthistorisches,albertina" limit="6"]

Getting there, and when

  • Tram D runs from the Ring, past the Opera, to the stop Schloss Belvedere, beside the Upper Belvedere. The main railway station is about ten minutes away on foot.
  • Start at the top and walk down through the garden to the Lower Belvedere, where tram 71 takes you back to the Ring.
  • The first slot of the morning and the last hour and a half are the calmest in front of The Kiss.
  • The Kunsthistorisches Museum is closed on Mondays for much of the year.

Current hours are on our pages for the Belvedere, the Kunsthistorisches Museum and the Albertina.

From here

More of Klimt is a short walk from the Opera: the Beethoven Frieze he painted in 1902 is in the basement of the Secession, the white building with the golden dome of leaves. For the rest of Vienna, or to fit the city into a longer trip, open the trip planner for Austria.

Cover photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Where is Klimt's Kiss in Vienna?
faqs.a: In the Upper Belvedere, on the upper floor, among the largest collection of Klimt paintings anywhere. The gallery does not lend it, so Vienna is the only place to see it.

faqs.q: Is The Kiss in the Upper or the Lower Belvedere?
faqs.a: In the Upper Belvedere, which holds the permanent collection. The Lower Belvedere shows temporary exhibitions and Belvedere 21 shows contemporary art, each on its own ticket unless a combined one is bought.

faqs.q: Are the Belvedere gardens free?
faqs.a: Yes. The garden between the Upper and the Lower Belvedere is free to walk. Only the buildings need a ticket.

faqs.q: Kunsthistorisches Museum or Albertina: which one?
faqs.a: The Kunsthistorisches Museum for old masters, above all Bruegel, Vermeer, Raphael and Velázquez, and it needs at least two hours. The Albertina is shorter: palace state rooms and modern painting from Monet to Picasso.

faqs.q: How long does the Upper Belvedere take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for The Kiss, the other Klimt and Schiele rooms and the Marble Hall. Add half an hour to walk down through the garden.

title: Mozart's Salzburg on foot: a route through the old town, and what is free along it
subtitle: Two houses, a font, a mass, three graves. Most of the walk costs nothing, and it helps to know which doors do.
excerpt: A walking route through Salzburg in Mozart's footsteps, from the house where he was born to the Mirabell gardens, with what is free on the way, what needs a ticket, and what the partner's audio walks include.
secondary_keywords: what is free in Salzburg old town
longtail_phrases: how to see Mozart's Salzburg on foot
what is free to see in Salzburg old town
is Mozart's birthplace worth visiting
where is the Mozart family buried in Salzburg
how long does it take to walk Salzburg old town
meta_title: Mozart's Salzburg on foot: route, and what is free
meta_description: A walk through Salzburg from Mozart's birthplace to the Mirabell gardens: what is free, which doors need a ticket, and what the audio walks include.

featured_image.alt: The domes and roofs of the old town of Salzburg with the fortress on its hill and mountains behind

content_html:
[place attraction="mozart-s-birthplace" city="salzburg"]

For half a century after his death, Salzburg did very little about Mozart. He had left the town in 1781 after a quarrel with its ruler, the prince-archbishop, and had died in Vienna ten years later. When a committee at last collected money for a statue, the workmen digging its foundation in 1841 struck a Roman mosaic floor, and the unveiling had to wait a year.

The bronze figure was finally shown on 4 September 1842, in the square that now bears his name. His two sons were in the crowd. His widow Constanze, who had lived in a house on that same square, had died six months earlier. Today the whole old town trades on him, and the visitor has the opposite problem: sorting the places where Mozart really lived and worked from the chocolate, and knowing which of them cost nothing to see.

How the old town is laid out

Salzburg's old town is a narrow strip between the river Salzach and a wall of rock, the Mönchsberg, with the fortress on a hill at one end. Almost all of it is closed to traffic, and you can cross it in fifteen minutes. A second, smaller old quarter lies across the river, with the Mirabell gardens. The route below takes two to three hours without going inside anything, and half a day with one museum.

The route, stop by stop

1. Getreidegasse 9, the birthplace

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born on 27 January 1756 on the third floor of the tall yellow house at number 9, where his parents rented a flat for twenty-six years. It has been a museum since 1880 and needs a ticket: inside are the family rooms, portraits, letters and the violin he played as a child. The street itself, with its wrought-iron guild signs and the passages that run through the houses to the next street, is free.

Getreidegasse 9. The Mozarts rented the third floor. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

2. Alter Markt

The old market square has two institutions. Café Tomaselli is the oldest coffee house in the town. Opposite, the confectioner Fürst still makes by hand the Mozartkugel that Paul Fürst invented in 1890, wrapped in silver and blue. The red and gold ones sold everywhere else are later copies.

3. Residenzplatz and Mozartplatz

The largest square, with its baroque fountain, lies between the old and the new palace of the archbishops. The bells in the tower of the new palace play a tune three times a day, at seven, eleven and six. The statue of 1842 is on the smaller square next door. All of this is free.

Residenzplatz: the fountain, and on the right the tower whose bells play three times a day. Photo: DimiTalen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

4. The cathedral

Mozart was baptised here the day after he was born, at the bronze font that still stands to the left of the entrance, and from 1779 he was the cathedral's organist. Outside the hours of services, visitors are now asked for an entry contribution.

5. St Peter's: the church, the cemetery, the catacombs

In the abbey church of St Peter, on 26 October 1783, Mozart conducted the first performance of his Mass in C minor, with Constanze singing one of the soprano parts. The church is free. So is the cemetery behind it, the oldest in the town, where his sister Nannerl is buried. The small chambers cut into the rock face above the graves, known as the catacombs, charge a small fee.

St Peter's cemetery, with the catacombs cut into the rock above the arcades. Photo: Isiwal, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Across the river: the Mozart Residence

Cross by the footbridge. In 1773 the family moved to a larger flat in the Dancing Master's House on what is now Makartplatz, and Mozart lived there until he left for Vienna. Half the house was destroyed by a bomb in 1944 and rebuilt in the 1990s. It is the second Mozart museum, with its own ticket and a combined one with the birthplace.

7. The Mirabell gardens

The gardens of the palace an archbishop built in 1606 are free, and the view from the steps at their northern end runs straight across the flower beds to the fortress. The young Mozarts played for the court in the palace's Marble Hall, which is now the town's wedding room.

The Mirabell gardens, with the fortress at the end of the view. Photo: Isiwal, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Free, and not free

  • Free: Getreidegasse and its passages, the squares and the bells, St Peter's church and cemetery, the Mirabell gardens, the walk up to the fortress walls.
  • Ticket: the two Mozart houses, the cathedral outside services, the catacombs, the fortress and its funicular.
  • One ticket for several: the DomQuartier is a single circuit through the archbishops' state rooms, where the boy Mozart performed, their picture gallery, the gallery above the cathedral's nave and the museum of St Peter's.

If you pay for only one Mozart house, choose the birthplace for the feeling of the rooms, the Residence for space and fewer people.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The audio walks through the old town, the baroque churches and the Mirabell quarter are commentary in the partner's app, with a map. None of them includes entry anywhere. One states plainly that the ticket to Mozart's birthplace is extra.
  • The walk "from High Baroque to the Catacombs" takes you into three churches, and warns that they may be shut early in the morning and in the evening.
  • The DomQuartier entry ticket is the one listing with entry. It has no audio from the partner, and its page gives few details.
  • The partner also lists day trips from Salzburg into Bavaria. They are not about the town.

These are the audio walks and tickets our partner sells in Salzburg, with today's prices:

[partner city="salzburg" match="old town,walk,domquartier,mirabell" limit="6"]

When to go

Getreidegasse is packed from late morning to mid afternoon, when the day coaches are in. Walk it before ten or after five. The town is at its fullest, and its dearest, during the festival in July and August. Hours of the museums are on our pages for Mozart's birthplace and the DomQuartier.

From here

The Hohensalzburg Fortress, begun in 1077, is above you the whole way: a funicular climbs to it from the lane behind the cathedral, or you can walk up in about twenty minutes. Mozart's father Leopold and his widow Constanze lie in the cemetery of St Sebastian, across the river on Linzer Gasse, which is free and almost always empty. See what else there is in Salzburg, or open the attractions map of Austria.

Cover photo: Uoaei1, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you see Mozart's Salzburg on foot?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town is small and mostly closed to traffic. A route from the birthplace on Getreidegasse to the Mirabell gardens takes two to three hours without going inside, or half a day with one museum.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Salzburg old town?
faqs.a: Getreidegasse and its passages, Residenzplatz and the bells of its tower, Mozartplatz, St Peter's church and cemetery and the Mirabell gardens. The Mozart houses, the catacombs, the fortress and the DomQuartier need a ticket.

faqs.q: Mozart's birthplace or the Mozart Residence: which one?
faqs.a: The birthplace on Getreidegasse has the rooms where he was born and is the more crowded. The Residence across the river, where the family lived from 1773, is larger and quieter. A combined ticket covers both.

faqs.q: Is Mozart buried in Salzburg?
faqs.a: No. Mozart was buried in Vienna. In Salzburg his sister Nannerl lies in St Peter's cemetery, and his father Leopold and his widow Constanze in the cemetery of St Sebastian.

faqs.q: Do the audio walks of Salzburg include entry tickets?
faqs.a: No. The audio walks our partner sells are commentary with a map only. Entry to the Mozart houses, the fortress or the cathedral is bought separately.

title: Dresden's old town in a day: what is free to see, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: A church put back together stone by stone, a porcelain wall, a courtyard of pavilions, and the doors worth paying for.
excerpt: How to spend a day in Dresden's old town: the sights that cost nothing, from the Frauenkirche to the Procession of Princes, the museums worth a ticket in the Zwinger and the palace, and what the partner's walks include.
focus_keyword: what is free in Dresden old town
secondary_keywords: Dresden old town in one day
longtail_phrases: what to see in Dresden old town in one day
is the Frauenkirche in Dresden free
is the Zwinger in Dresden free
Historic Green Vault or New Green Vault
can you visit the Semperoper without seeing an opera
meta_title: Dresden's old town in a day: free and ticketed
meta_description: What costs nothing in the old town of Dresden, which museums in the Zwinger and the palace are worth a ticket, and how to walk it all in a day.

featured_image.alt: The lit skyline of the old town of Dresden at night, seen across the river Elbe

content_html:
[place attraction="zwinger-dresden" city="dresden"]

The Frauenkirche survived the bombing of Dresden, at first. On the night of 13 February 1945 the fire burned all around it and inside it, and its stone dome still stood the next day. On the morning of 15 February the glowing pillars could carry the weight no longer, and the church fell in on itself.

For forty-five years the heap of blackened stones lay in the middle of the city, left there as a memorial. After 1990 it was taken apart, each stone was measured and numbered, and from 1994 the church was built again to the old plans, with the surviving pieces set back in their places. It was consecrated on 30 October 2005. You can read the story on the walls: the dark stones are the old ones. Most of the old town around it was put back in the same way, and much of what makes Dresden worth a day can be seen without a ticket.

How the old town is laid out

Everything in this guide lies within ten minutes' walk, on the south bank of the Elbe. From west to east: the Zwinger, the opera on Theaterplatz, the Catholic cathedral, the royal palace, the terrace above the river, and the Frauenkirche on the Neumarkt. The main railway station is a quarter of an hour to the south on foot, along the pedestrian Prager Strasse.

What costs nothing

  • The Frauenkirche. Entry to the church is free when no service or concert is on, and a donation is welcome. The climb to the platform on top of the dome is a separate ticket. The golden cross on the summit was made by a London goldsmith whose father flew in the raid, and was given by Britain.
  • The Procession of Princes. On the outer wall of the palace stables, 102 metres of Saxon rulers on horseback, made of some 23,000 tiles of Meissen porcelain between 1904 and 1907. It came through the bombing almost unharmed.
  • Brühl's Terrace. The promenade on top of the old river wall, known as the Balcony of Europe, reached by a broad stair from the palace square.
  • The courtyard of the Zwinger. The pavilions, the Crown Gate and the fountains can be walked through freely, though parts of the court have been under restoration.
  • The Catholic cathedral. Built for a court that had turned Catholic in a Lutheran city. The heart of Augustus the Strong is kept in its crypt. His body is in Kraków.
  • The view from the other bank. Cross the Augustus Bridge and look back: this is the skyline that Bernardo Bellotto, called Canaletto, painted in 1748.

The stone dome of the Frauenkirche, rebuilt between 1994 and 2005. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Procession of Princes, on the outer wall of the palace stables. Photo: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What needs a ticket, and which to choose

The Zwinger museums

The Zwinger was built between 1710 and 1728 by the architect Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann and the sculptor Balthasar Permoser for Augustus the Strong, as an orangery and a setting for court festivals. Three museums are in its wings. The one to choose is the Old Masters Picture Gallery: Raphael's Sistine Madonna, with the two bored angels at the bottom, Giorgione's Sleeping Venus, and Vermeer's Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window, on whose back wall a painted Cupid, hidden for centuries, was uncovered in a restoration finished in 2021. The other two are the porcelain collection and a cabinet of old scientific instruments.

The Crown Gate of the Zwinger, with the Polish crown on top. Photo: Avi1111 dr. avishai teicher, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The royal palace and the two Green Vaults

The treasury of the Saxon electors, opened to visitors by Augustus the Strong in the 1720s, is shown in two parts, and they are easy to confuse.

  • The Historic Green Vault is the suite of baroque rooms on the ground floor, rebuilt as they were, with the objects standing free on gilded brackets. Numbers are limited and the ticket is for a fixed time. It often sells out.
  • The New Green Vault, upstairs, shows single masterpieces in glass cases, with good light: the Dresden Green Diamond, a cherry stone carved with dozens of faces, and a miniature court of the Grand Mogul made of gold and enamel. It is included in the general palace ticket.

In November 2019 thieves broke into the historic rooms and took several sets of jewels. Much of the loot was recovered three years later.

The Semperoper

Gottfried Semper's opera house burned in 1869, was rebuilt to his plans by 1878, was destroyed in 1945 and reopened on 13 February 1985. You do not need an opera ticket to see inside: guided visits run by day, when rehearsals allow.

The Semperoper on Theaterplatz, with King John of Saxony on his horse. Photo: Robert von Oliva (naruciakk), via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

A day, in order

  • Morning: the Zwinger courtyard, then two hours in the picture gallery.
  • Midday: Theaterplatz, the cathedral, the Procession of Princes, and the Neumarkt for the Frauenkirche.
  • Afternoon: a Green Vault, or a guided visit to the opera.
  • Evening: Brühl's Terrace, then the bridge, for the view back in the last light.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Semperoper entry and guided visit with an audio city walk pairs a visit inside the opera house, led by a guide in person, with an audio walk through the old town. Its list of inclusions names only the audio part, so read the page for the times and the language of the visit.
  • The audio walks of the baroque centre are commentary in the partner's app with a map. They pass the Zwinger, the Frauenkirche and the palace from outside, and tickets to anything on the way are not included.
  • TimeRide Dresden is a separate indoor attraction that shows the baroque city in virtual reality. It is not one of the monuments.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells in Dresden, with today's prices:

[partner city="dresden" match="semperoper,entry,guided,frauenkirche" limit="6"]

Practical notes

The museums of the Zwinger and those of the palace close on different days of the week, so one of the two is always open. Check which before you fix your day: current hours are on our pages for the Zwinger and the Green Vault.

From here

Across the bridge, the Neustadt is the part of Dresden that did not burn: a long avenue under plane trees, then streets of cafés and courtyards. Paddle steamers leave from the quay below Brühl's Terrace for the palace of Pillnitz, upriver. For the rest of Dresden, or a route through Saxony, open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Gaurav Chingale, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Frauenkirche in Dresden free?
faqs.a: Entry to the church is free when no service or concert is taking place, and a donation is welcome. The climb to the viewing platform on the dome needs a separate ticket.

faqs.q: Is the Zwinger in Dresden free?
faqs.a: The courtyard, with its pavilions, gate and fountains, is free to walk through. The three museums in its wings, among them the Old Masters Picture Gallery, need a ticket.

faqs.q: Historic Green Vault or New Green Vault: which one?
faqs.a: The Historic Green Vault is the suite of baroque treasury rooms, with limited numbers and a timed ticket. The New Green Vault shows single masterpieces in cases and is part of the general palace ticket. With little time, the New one is easier to get into.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Semperoper without seeing an opera?
faqs.a: Yes. Guided visits of the building run by day when rehearsals allow, on their own ticket.

faqs.q: Can you see Dresden old town in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. The sights lie within ten minutes of each other on foot. A day is enough for the free sights, one museum in the Zwinger and either a Green Vault or a visit to the opera house.

title: The Elbphilharmonie Plaza and Hamburg's harbour on foot: how the Plaza ticket works, and a route
subtitle: You can go up the concert hall without a concert. Then three kilometres of quays, ships and brick warehouses.
excerpt: How to visit the Plaza of the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg without a concert ticket, and a walking route along the harbour from the Landungsbrücken to the Speicherstadt, with what is free and what the partner's listings include.
longtail_phrases: can you visit the Elbphilharmonie without a concert ticket
how does the Elbphilharmonie Plaza ticket work
how to walk from Landungsbrücken to Speicherstadt
what is free to see in Hamburg harbour
is the Old Elbe Tunnel free
meta_title: Elbphilharmonie Plaza and Hamburg harbour on foot
meta_description: Visit the Elbphilharmonie Plaza without a concert, then walk the harbour from the Landungsbrücken to the Speicherstadt. What is free, what needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The curved glass facade of the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg rising above the brick walls of the old warehouse

content_html:
[place attraction="rickmer-rickmers" city="hamburg"]

At the western point of Hamburg's old docks stood a plain brick warehouse, built in the 1960s to store cocoa, tea and tobacco. By the end of the century nobody needed it. The city's plan was to stand a concert hall of glass on top of the brick box, designed by the Swiss architects Herzog and de Meuron, and to open it in 2010.

It opened on 11 January 2017. By then the cost to the city had grown to about ten times the first estimate, and the building had spent years as Germany's favourite example of a public project gone wrong. Then people saw it finished, and forgave it. Between the brick below and the glass above the architects left a gap, one whole floor open to the weather on every side, 37 metres over the water. This is the Plaza, and you do not need a concert ticket to stand on it.

How the Plaza works

The Plaza is a public viewing floor, with a walkway that runs all the way round the outside of the building. You get in with a Plaza ticket, issued for a time, because the number of people allowed up at once is limited. There are two ways to have one: book it in advance for a fixed slot, or ask at the building on the day, when places are left. On summer weekends and around sunset, they often are not.

From the entrance, a curved escalator about eighty metres long carries you up through the old warehouse. It bends, so you cannot see the top from the bottom. It lets you out at a large window facing down the river, and a second, short escalator brings you to the Plaza.

What the Plaza ticket does not include is the concert halls. To see the great hall, with its terraces of seats wrapped round the stage, you need a concert ticket or a place on one of the house's guided tours, which sell out early. Anyone with a concert ticket can go up to the Plaza before the performance.

Looking inland from the Plaza: the brick of the warehouse district, and the spires of the city behind. Photo: Mathieu Chollet, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A route along the harbour

The walk below is about three kilometres, flat, and takes two to three hours with the Plaza. Underground line U3 runs above ground along this stretch of the harbour, with stops at the Landungsbrücken and at Baumwall, beside the concert hall.

1. The Landungsbrücken

Start at the long terminal building with the green domes, finished in 1909, and the floating pontoons below it, where the liners once tied up. Harbour ferries leave from here, and they are part of the city's public transport, so an ordinary day ticket is good for a ride down the river and back. At the western end a domed hall holds the lifts and stairs down to the Old Elbe Tunnel of 1911, which pedestrians cross free of charge to a view of the whole waterfront from the other bank.

2. Two museum ships

Moored along the quay are the Rickmer Rickmers, a three-masted sailing ship built in 1896, with a green hull, and further on the Cap San Diego, a white cargo ship of 1961. Both are museums with their own tickets. Looking at them from the quay is free.

The Rickmer Rickmers at her mooring, and behind her the tower of St Michael's. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. The promenade to the Elbphilharmonie

The riverside walk between the ships and the concert hall is also the city's flood wall, rebuilt to a design by Zaha Hadid, with wide steps where people sit facing the water. The Elbphilharmonie is in front of you the whole way.

4. The HafenCity

Behind the concert hall begins the HafenCity, a whole new district built on old dock land since the early 2000s. Its ground was raised by several metres, so that the streets stay dry when storm tides flood the quays. The Magellan Terraces step down to a basin of historic boats.

The Magellan Terraces, stepping down to the old Sandtorhafen. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

5. The Speicherstadt

End among the red brick warehouses built from 1883 on thousands of oak piles, where coffee, tea, spices and carpets were stored free of customs duty. Some twenty thousand people lost their homes to make room for it. The warehouses and their canals have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2015. The picture everyone takes is of the Wasserschloss, the small turreted building on a point between two canals, seen from the bridge to its east.

The Wasserschloss, where two canals of the Speicherstadt meet. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Free, and not free

  • Free: the quays and the promenade, the Old Elbe Tunnel on foot, the streets and bridges of the Speicherstadt and the HafenCity.
  • Ticket: the Plaza, the two museum ships, and the museums inside the warehouses, of which Miniatur Wunderland, the giant model railway, needs booking days ahead.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Elbphilharmonie Plaza ticket with a HafenCity audio tour includes a ticket for the Plaza and an audio walk through the Speicherstadt and the HafenCity in the partner's app. The concert halls are not included.
  • The same audio tour "without a ticket" is the commentary alone. You arrange your own Plaza ticket.
  • The Rickmer Rickmers ticket with a city audio tour includes entry to the ship and an audio walk through the city. There is no commentary on board.
  • The other audio walks, of the HafenCity, the harbour and maritime Hamburg, are commentary with a map. Tickets to anything on the way are extra.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells for the harbour of Hamburg, with today's prices:

[partner city="hamburg" match="elbphilharmonie,hafencity,rickmer,harbor,maritime" limit="6"]

When to go

The Plaza is at its best in the hour before sunset, when the light comes up the river, and that is when slots go first. It is windy up there in any season: bring a layer. The Speicherstadt is lit after dark, and looks its best then. Hours of the ship are on our page for the Rickmer Rickmers.

From here

The tower you see behind the ships is St Michael's Church, the sailors' landmark, ten minutes uphill from the Landungsbrücken, with a platform near the top that looks back over everything you have walked. The town hall and the Alster lake are a quarter of an hour north of the Speicherstadt. See what else there is in Hamburg, or open the attractions map of Germany.

Cover photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Elbphilharmonie without a concert ticket?
faqs.a: Yes. The Plaza, the open viewing floor 37 metres above the water, can be visited with a Plaza ticket for a time slot. The concert halls themselves need a concert ticket or a guided tour of the house.

faqs.q: How does the Elbphilharmonie Plaza ticket work?
faqs.a: It is issued for a time, because numbers on the Plaza are limited. You can book one in advance for a fixed slot, or ask at the building on the day when places are left.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from the Landungsbrücken to the Speicherstadt?
faqs.a: About three kilometres along the river, past the museum ships and the Elbphilharmonie and through the HafenCity. Allow two to three hours with a visit to the Plaza.

faqs.q: Is the Old Elbe Tunnel free?
faqs.a: Pedestrians cross the Old Elbe Tunnel free of charge. Lifts and stairs go down from the domed hall at the western end of the Landungsbrücken.

faqs.q: Does the Plaza ticket include the concert hall?
faqs.a: No. A Plaza ticket covers the viewing floor and the walkway round the building. The great hall can be seen only at a concert or on a guided tour.
